task.goal: Compile the MEM-REL-Relatable single-frame quote-card format (persona tweet header + reaction photo + caption/statistic overlay) into a governed SuperVisuals structural contract.
task.success_condition: The compiled structural contract preserves the persona header block, the single reaction image with its overlay text or speech-bubble quote, and every wrong_reading_lock intact and unweakened.
task.atomic_boundary: One ratified relatable-moment concept becomes exactly one single-frame structural contract; no multi-slide sequencing, video timeline, or animation frame series is produced.

source_expression_moment.description: The specific relatable football-fan pain point, jab, or in-joke this instance dramatizes, e.g. an injury setback, a transfer/sponsor jab, or an academy-release fear.

voice_context.description: The persona's caption register for this instance: phrasing, emoji use, and fan vernacular consistent with the branded account voice observed in the specimens.

activative_input.hidden_pressure: The audience wants to feel privately recognized inside a shared football-fan wound (injury heartbreak, sponsor cynicism, academy rejection) without admitting vulnerability outright; tagging a friend or laughing at the caption lets them point at the feeling instead of naming it.
activative_input.stance: Wry, communal, and self-deprecating on behalf of the whole fan base — never mocking the individual tagged friend, only the shared situation.
stakes: keep the joke legible as fan commentary, not real news
avoid implying a real, identifiable person actually said the caption
activative_input.participation_design: One-tap resonance: the viewer either tags a friend the caption fits, reacts, or shares; no further commitment is asked of them.
activative_input.intended_reaction: The viewer laughs in recognition, tags a friend the caption fits, and associates the persona account with 'gets our world.'
activative_input.smallest_useful_commitment: Tag one friend, or leave one reaction.
wrong_reading_locks: Do not let the composited tweet-card (persona avatar, handle, verified badge) be mistaken for an authentic captured screenshot of a real posted tweet — it must stay legible as a designed quote-card template, not evidence of a real utterance.

Do not let any real, named public figure's photo used in a reaction-template layout be read as if that person authored, endorsed, or spoke the overlaid caption; it must read as fan commentary about them, never as their own statement.

Do not let the photorealistic anonymous subject in a first-person quote bubble be mistaken for a real, identifiable individual making a real factual claim — the figure is an illustrative composite, not a sourced testimonial.

Do not let a bold on-image statistic be read as sourced or verified reporting; it is a dramatized emotional hook and must not be paired with a real club or player's name without explicit satire framing.
Do not let a real brand name used in a sponsor-swap joke be read as an announced or confirmed sponsorship deal; it must remain legible as speculation, not news.
